subject: Copywriting
title: A/B Testing Subject Lines
description: A short lesson to help you apply A/B Testing Subject Lines.

hook.text: Obama's 2012 campaign raised $690 million by email. The winning subject line? 'Hey.' Tested against 17 variations.

buildup.text: A/B testing sends two subject lines to small segments. The winner goes to the full list. Data picks the champion.

discovery.text: Small changes produce big swings. Adding a single emoji can lift opens 15%. Removing one word can double clicks.

twist.text: Testing one variable at a time is critical. Testing subject AND sender AND time simultaneously proves nothing.

climax.text: The brands that test relentlessly—like Amazon, Netflix, and BuzzFeed—build subject line intelligence that compounds.

punchline.text: 'Hey' raised $690 million. Test everything. Instincts lie.

quiz.question: What was the winning subject line in Obama's 2012 email campaign?

details.summary: A/B testing subject lines sends two variants to small segments of your list, then sends the winner to the rest. This simple technique consistently improves open rates by 10-30%. details.whyItMatters: Subject line testing turns email copy from guesswork into science. Small improvements in open rates compound across every campaign, dramatically increasing total revenue over time.
takeaways: Send two variants to small segments, then deploy the winner to all
Isolate one variable per test for clear, actionable results
Even a 5% improvement in open rates compounds significantly over time

faq.question: How large should A/B test segments be?
faq.answer: Typically 10-15% of your list per variant. Too small and results are unreliable; too large and you lose the benefit of sending the winner to the majority. Most email platforms calculate optimal sample sizes automatically.

faq.question: What subject line elements should be tested first?
faq.answer: Start with the highest-impact variables: curiosity versus direct benefit, short versus long, personalized versus generic, and question versus statement. These fundamental differences typically produce the largest performance gaps in early tests.
